newsitem.title: FRANCE: Top French researcher warns against clone panic.
newsitem.headline: Top French researcher warns against clone panic.

text.p: France's agricultural research chief has warned against panic over the cloning of an adult sheep, saying that although human clones may be possible one day it was urgent to prevent such experiments happening.

Guy Paillotin, president of the National Institute for Agricultural Research (INRA), a state-funded research agency, said news of the experiment by Scottish researchers was "whipping up panic" by raising the prospect that similar experiments could be performed on humans.
"It is obvious that we can no longer say that (human cloning) is impossible. But in ethical terms it isn't a conceivable application," Paillotin told Reuters in an interview late on Wednesday.
"We must definitely place strict controls on how this research is applied," he said.
Researchers at the Roslin Institute near Edinburgh disclosed on Sunday that they had successfully cloned a sheep from the cell of another adult sheep.
On Thursday, a British government-appointed committee set up to track genetic science held its first meeting and its chairman said fears over cloning would be high on the agenda.
U.S. President Bill Clinton has also ordered a rapid ethical inquiry into the latest discoveries.
Paillotin said real scientific issues were already being sidetracked by "stupid" talk of mad scientists cloning humans.

"The (cloning) itself must be dissociated from the way in which we will apply our knowledge of biological development," he said. "Everyone thinks that it will be used to clone a human. That's what is creating the confusion."

"We must say very loudly that this is out of the question, that this is stupid," he added. "Man is unique because most of its intelligence comes essentially from education, culture, though of course genes do play a part."
Cloning fascinated the public but was not necessarily the most interested application of new genetic technology, he said.
"Finding out how a cell develops, how it is programmed, how it can go backwards -- these are issues involved in cancer so they are very important," he said.

INRA is also involved in genetic research and has managed to clone calves from embryo cells, an earlier type of cloning developed in Britain last year and which paved the way for the first adult sheep clone this week.
